national.title: Seven students killed and nearly 100 injured in explosion in Afghanistan, official says
national.summary: A spokesman for Afhganistan's interior ministry says the blast was caused by carelessness at an explosives depot nearby.
national.body:
At least seven students have been killed and 99 others have been injured following an explosion near a school in Afghanistan, an official has said.

The incident happened on Saturday morning in the Anderseir area of Asadabad, the capital of Kunar province, a spokesperson for the Taliban government's interior ministry said.

Posting on X, Abdul Mateen Qani said that according to initial investigations, the blast was caused by "negligence and carelessness" at an explosives depot belonging to nearby mining companies.

national.title: New wave of Democratic attorneys general may reshape the justice system
national.summary: The Democratic victories could have major effects for what alleged crimes are investigated, lawsuits filed and court cases heard across the U.S.
national.body:
Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson, a Democrat, is seen speaking on the state Senate floor in Austin on Sept. 3, 2025. Eric Gay/AP hide caption

The nation's legal landscape is set for a major shift after voters elected Democrats to serve as attorney general in five formerly Republican-led states. That means a majority of states will soon have a Democrat serving as the top law enforcement officer.

Democratic candidates flipped attorneys general offices in Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas–and in Alaska, the incoming Democratic governor announced his pick for attorney general in a state previously run by Republicans.

The Democratic victories could have major effects for what alleged crimes are investigated, lawsuits filed and court cases heard across the U.S. State attorneys general typically have sweeping discretion in what legal challenges to bring or drop on behalf of their state's residents.

And with roughly seven in ten Americans set to live in a state with a Democratic attorney general, Democrats will be able to bring many more cases across the country that argue for their positions on the economy, environment, abortion, civil rights, and crime, rather than the Republican perspective.

"Voters picked AGs who will stand up and fight for them, whether that's taking on rising costs, pushing back against a lawless administration, or holding bad actors accountable. It's a time to celebrate, and also to get to work," Democratic Attorneys General Association President Sean Rankin said in a statement to NPR.

Conversely, the midterm election defeats for Republicans attorneys general candidates left the conservative legal movement reeling – and planning a comeback.

"There's no sugarcoating it, this was the worst election for Republicans since 1974," said Adam Piper, executive director of the Republican Attorneys General Association.

national.title: Australian wrestler Bronson Reed dies aged 38, WWE says
national.summary: Tributes have flooded in for the 38-year-old Australian who is survived by his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter.
national.body:
Professional wrestler Bronson Reed has died aged 38, World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE) has announced.

The company said the wrestler, whose real name is Jermaine Haley, died on Friday due to medical complications but did not give further details.

Paying tribute, WWE added: "Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague."

They also offered condolences to the Australian's family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, and their daughter.

Haley was honoured at the WWE event at Akins Ford Arena in Athens, Georgia on Friday.

The show began with a 10-bell salute for Haley and in his match, Canadian wrestler Kevin Owens wore an armband that read "Bronson" and addressed the crowd.

"I knew for a fact, beyond performing in this ring, he loved his family more than anything so tonight if there is anything to take away from a tragedy like that - it's take care of each other and love each other... Forgive each other," Owens said.

"Bronson, for me, we were lucky to have you and you will be extremely missed."

national.title: Two staff killed in Israeli strike on Gaza medical clinic, MSF says
national.summary: The Israeli military says it targeted "Hamas terrorists" in the strike which has been condemned by the World Health Organization.
national.body:
Two workers for the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have been killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza, according to the organisation.

MSF said the strike was a direct hit on one of the charity's clinics, the location of which was known by the Israeli military.

In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the two people were Hamas operatives "acting as security guards at a clinic operated by MSF". The IDF added the strike was "not directed at a hospital" and caused no damage to medical infrastructure.

The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said that attacks on health facilities and health workers in Gaza were "outrageous and unacceptable".

In a post on X, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote: "Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked."

In its statement, MSF - which is also known as Doctors Without Borders - said that the two workers who were killed were watchmen, and added that the strike brought the number of its colleagues killed in Gaza to 17.

The organisation said it was "devastated and outraged" and added: "​Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military."

In its own post on X, the IDF said that the two men, who they named as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, were "terrorists in Hamas' military wing".

national.title: Eight killed in Peruvian military helicopter crash
national.summary: The pilot was the sole survivor of the crash during a rescue mission in a remote area known for drug trafficking.
national.body:
Eight military personnel have been killed in a helicopter crash in a remote area of Peru known for growing and trafficking drugs.

Authorities say the aircraft came down near the town of Sanabamba during a mission to evacuate an army patrol in the valley of the Apurimac, Ene, and Mantaro rivers, known by its Spanish acronym VRAEM.

Often referred to as 'Cocaine Valley', the area is Peru's largest coca-growing valley where gangs and the remnants of the former Shining Path rebel group operate.

The Peruvian ministry of defence said the pilot was the sole survivor of the crash, the cause of which is still unknown.

In its statement, the ministry said "search and rescue operations located the aircraft and the nine military personnel who were on board".

It named the pilot as Enzo Espinoza Roque and said he was evacuated to Lima to "receive specialised medical treatment".

The aircraft was reported missing on Thursday night after rescuing three army personnel.

No further information was shared about why the group needed to be rescued, but it was confirmed that they were among those who were killed in the crash.

national.title: Turkish officials 'destroyed' pro-opposition TV channel, owner tells BBC
national.summary: The headquarters of Halk TV were raided last month, the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed critical of the government.
national.body:
Turkish authorities have "destroyed" one of the country's most-watched news channels, its London-based owner has told the BBC.

Speaking to the BBC's Newshour, Cafer Mahiroğlu said that nine people connected to Halk TV were arrested this week on charges including money laundering, bribery and spreading misleading information.

Mahiroğlu said that several of his family members were among those arrested when the pro-opposition channel was taken into government control last month, adding that the allegations against him and Halk TV are "completely wrong".

The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor' Office said that two former news anchors of the channel were among the most recent group of people detained.

In a statement, prosecutors accused the anchors of producing "false reports" in exchange for money.

Authorities have also issued an arrest warrant for the channel's news coordinator Kürşad Oğuz who is "abroad", the statement said, without specifying where.

Mahiroğlu told the BBC that he could be sent to prison if he tried to return to Turkey.

"[The government] wants to be in control of the whole media... I'm more worried about my country and my democracy than my channel," he said.

national.summary: Heavy rain over flooded East Coast communities began easing Friday, and power was slowly restored to hundreds of thousands of customers.
national.body: Heavy rain over flooded East Coast communities began easing Friday, and power was slowly restored to hundreds of thousands of customers as some places stayed on guard for high-tide flooding following a round of holiday storms.The storms snarled travel and downed trees and power lines. The heavy weather led to water rescues from New York to Virginia. In New York City, preparations were underway to hold Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade on Saturday after an unprecedented postponement because of rain and high winds.Elsewhere, wet snow fell as far south as the Tennessee Valley and freezing rain moved across northern New England. Cold rain was reported in parts of the Midwest, including the Ohio Valley and the lower Great Lakes.Another storm system in the Northwest brought rain along coastal Oregon. More snow was forecast in the Cascade Range and in mountain passes in Montana and Wyoming.There were just under 3,700 flights in the U.S. delayed as of Friday night, with another 162 canceled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware.The number of power outages, which peaked Thursday at more than 900,000 customers, fell to just under 300,000 by Friday night, according to utility tracker PowerOutage.us.Bad weather in the East is taking its time to goConditions were expected to improve Friday across the entire eastern U.S., "but this huge system will take some time to weaken," the National Weather Service said on its website. national.title: U.S. Air Force cloud platform breached by hackers, report says
national.summary: The alleged incident follows a series of breaches and outages that have been reported at federal agencies this month.
national.body: The U.S. Air Force's cloud computing platform was breached in a cyberattack, multiple sources told Reuters on Friday.The hackers breached Cloud One, the Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, according to Reuters, potentially exposing sensitive military and personnel information.The breach was discovered at some point in the last month during system upgrades, sources told the outlet. In a statement provided to CBS News, an Air Force spokesperson did not confirm or deny the breach, saying that it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities, or operational status of specific networks and systems.""Ensuring the security, resilience and availability of our most critical war fighting assets remains a top priority," the Air Force spokesperson said. In a follow-up statement, the Defense Department said that its systems "are safe, secure, and managed 24-7 by the best experts and teams in the world," adding that it "will continue to maintain all mission-critical operations and applications."When reached by CBS News, Leidos, the tech company which has served as the main contractor operating Cloud One since May, declined to comment specifically on the hack, deferring to the Air Force. A Leidos spokesperson noted that earlier this year, it announced a $454.9 million contract to modernize and secure the Air Force's cloud operations.The alleged incident follows a series of breaches and outages that have been reported at federal agencies this month, including at the National Security Agency, the CIA, the FBI, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, and the Federal Aviation Administration, the latter of which prompted a nationwide ground stop that triggered chaos for tens of thousands of travelers at U.S. airports.In the FBI breach reported last week, hackers accessed a large database used by law enforcement agencies nationwide to access criminal records. national.title: Hundreds of thousands still without power a day after US slammed with Thanksgiving storms
national.summary: Pennsylvania and neighbouring states remained badly affected on Friday after both coasts were lashed with wind and rain.
national.body:
More than 260,000 people remain without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.

Eastern areas were lashed on Thursday by a powerful storm which brought high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. Pennsylvania remained the state worst hit by power cuts early on Friday, according to monitoring site Poweroutage.us.

Conditions are now improving, though forecasters caution that it will take some time. The West Coast also was affected by its own storms.

Flight disruption persisted, too, with hundreds more delays and cancellations reported on Friday - another busy travel day.

More than 3,400 flights within, into, or out of the US were delayed and nearly 670 cancelled on Friday.

On Thanksgiving, more than 2,500 US flights were delayed and more than 450 were cancelled, according to Flightaware.com. One passenger told the BBC he had been stuck at New York's LaGuardia Airport for 13 hours while trying to fly to see friends in Chicago for Thanksgiving.

Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the East Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.

Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds, while waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk. On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport.

national.title: Two American Airlines planes clip wings before takeoff at Reagan airport in 'tense' moment
national.summary: No injuries were reported, and the FAA plans to investigate the incident, which occurred during taxiing.
national.body:
Two American Airlines jets hit each other at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport while taxiing for departure in Washington DC on Friday.

One jet "clipped the wing" of the other at around 5:10 ET (22:10 GMT), the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement. No injuries were reported, and the FAA plans to investigate.

Both aircraft returned to the gate and were removed from service to be inspected by maintenance teams, American Airlines said.

The incident happened at the same airport where 67 people died in a deadly collision between a jetliner and an Army helicopter in January 2025.

"American Airlines Flight 638 clipped the wing of American Airlines Flight 2152 while taxiing for departure," the FAA said.

Air traffic controllers can be heard on an audio recording saying two Boeing 737s clipped on the airport's runway. The controllers requested an emergency response and fire personnel to the plane, then directed the aircraft to return to the gate.

The "wingtips of both Boeing 737-800s made contact", American Airlines said in a statement. The airline added that it is working to get affected passengers who were evacuated from both planes to their destinations as soon as possible.

A passenger on flight 2152 headed to Chicago's O'Hare airport told the BBC that he felt a "large jolt" on the right side of the aircraft as they were taxiing before departure. The other plane, flight 638, was bound for Dallas-Fort Worth airport.

national.title: Nigeria's acting legend who was loved across Africa and beyond
national.summary: Before becoming a household name in the Nigerian film industry, Edochie built a career in broadcasting.
national.body:
For generations of Nigerians, Pete Edochie was more than a celebrated actor.

He was Okonkwo – the fierce, proud and troubled warrior whose portrayal in Things Fall Apart made him a household name and earned him a place in the hearts of millions.

Even in death, many Nigerians still refer to him by the character's name, a testament to the enduring impact of a role that defined his career.

Edochie died on 25 November, aged 79, in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.

In 1987, Edochie starred in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel. His portrayal of Okonkwo would change his life, establishing him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors and bringing him international recognition.

The series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.

Joy Nnamdi, a fan of both the novel and its television adaptation, believes Edochie was the perfect choice for the lead role.

She said nobody else could have brought the character to life as convincingly.

national.body: Hunger is expected to worsen in 16 countries over the next six months, with war-torn Sudan and Yemen among five nations facing the gravest risk, the United Nations' food agencies warned Friday. The agencies pointed to conflict, soaring fuel costs linked to war in the Middle East and steep cuts in aid. The Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Program's Hunger Hotspots report covers December through May 2026. It places Sudan, Yemen, South Sudan, Somalia and northern Nigeria at the highest level of concern. In Yemen, the report said, hunger is likely to worsen as fighting that resumed in July spreads across multiple fronts. All five have appeared on the list repeatedly since 2022. The Palestinian territories were moved down one level following the October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza, though 67% of Gaza's population still faces crisis-level hunger or worse, and the report warned that the gains were fragile. Yemen has been at war since 2014, when the Iran-backed Houthi rebels seized the capital, Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year. The Houthis' encirclement of the southwestern city of Taiz has created siege-like conditions there, and more than 300,000 people have been displaced since the escalation began in July, mostly in Taiz, Lahj and Aden provinces. In government-held areas, 1.8 million people face emergency levels of hunger, up from 1.6 million in the previous analysis. No recent assessment exists for areas held by the Houthis, which have become harder for aid groups to reach as the conflict has intensified. The last nationwide projection, which ran through February, found 18.3 million people, more than half the population, in crisis or worse. Yemen relies heavily on imported food and fuel, and the report warned that attacks on Red Sea shipping threaten that lifeline. Shipping is now disrupted in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and the Black Sea. Gulf fertilizer shipments remain largely halted.

national.title: 2 American Airlines jets clip wings on tarmac of Reagan Airport
national.summary: There were no injuries when the wingtips of two American Airlines jets made contact Friday evening on the tarmac of Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport outside Washington, D.C.
national.body: There were no injuries when the wingtips of two American Airlines jets made contact Friday evening on the tarmac of Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport outside Washington, D.C., officials said. American Airlines Flight 638 clipped the wing of American Airlines Flight 2152 a little after 5 p.m. local time while both aircraft were taxiing for departure, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. In a separate statement provided to CBS News, American Airlines said that both planes returned to their gates and were "removed from service for inspection by our maintenance team."Both the FAA and American Airlines said no injuries were reported.The Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority said in a statement that its fire and rescue personnel responded to both planes. The airports authority said there were no disruptions to any other flights.Flight 638 was bound for Dallas, while Flight 2152 was headed to Chicago. The airline said passengers would be placed on new planes and depart for their destinations later Friday night. Earlier this month, two passengers suffered minor injuries when the wingtip of a Copa Airlines jet struck the nose of a UPS cargo plane on the tarmac of Miami International Airport. And in early October, the left wingtip of a Delta Air Lines plane clipped the tail of an Air Canada aircraft on the tarmac of Los Angeles International Airport. There were no injuries. Reagan Airport has three runways, one of which is considered the busiest in the nation, and it operates with a tightly restricted airspace due to its location near the White House and Capitol Hill. In January 2025, an Army Black Hawk helicopter collided in midair with an American Airlines plane that was approaching to land at Reagan Airport. All 64 people aboard the American Airlines flight were killed, along with the three soldiers aboard the chopper.

national.title: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
national.summary: The Canadian man, who pleaded guilty to 14 counts of aiding and abetting suicide earlier this year, said he was remorseful for his actions.
national.body:
The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them.

Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term.

The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.

He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.

During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.

If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.

As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".

"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.

national.title: The Indian 'Tamasha queen' whose fans paid for a show that never happened
national.summary: A new Bollywood flim spotlights the remarkable life of dancer and singer Vithabhai Narayangaonkar.
national.body:
Few things could keep Vithabai Narayangaonkar, one of the greatest stars of Maharashtra's folk theatre, away from the stage.

In the 1960s, the singer, dancer and troupe leader was performing in Shikhar Shingnapur, a village in the western Indian state, when she went into labour.

"She quietly stepped behind the stage into a makeshift tent while the rest of us continued performing," her daughter, veteran folk artist Mangala Bansode, told BBC Marathi.

Outside, the restless audience kept shouting: "Where is Vitha?"

When Vithabai returned to the stage, she was cradling her newborn son, the seventh of her eight children.

"The audience was stunned, but they quietly left, saying, 'We will watch your performance later'," Bansode recalled.

Outspoken and quick-witted, Vithabai held audiences across Maharashtra in thrall for decades, earning the title of Tamasha Samradnyi – the empress of Tamasha, the state's traditional travelling folk theatre.

Now, more than two decades after her death, her life has inspired a Bollywood musical, Eetha, starring Shraddha Kapoor, and due for release on 4 December.

national.title: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
national.summary: While many people find a diagnosis for ADHD or autism affirming, a government-funded clinic in Sweden is re-assessing people who feel it does not reflect them.
national.body:
Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.

Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.

But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.

This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.

At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.

But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.

Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police.

"I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.

Nick Schifrin: We begin with the day's headlines. Tonight, crews are still working to restore power for hundreds of thousands of homes one day after that massive Thanksgiving Day storm forced some on the East Coast to dine in the dark. As of this evening, most of the lingering outages were in Pennsylvania and Missouri, where yesterday's nor'easter brought not only high winds, but also snow that toppled trees. In Delaware today, the rain had run its course, but trucks still trudged through flooded streets. And in New York City, workers are preparing for the postponed Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Tourists who came in from across the world say they're grateful the show will go on tomorrow. Woman: Well, at least it's going to happen on Saturday. So we cannot control the weather. national.summary: China's immense clout now also has the flex of soft power. Critics and dissidents say their voices are being drowned out.
national.body:
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.

"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."

It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.

But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.

It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .

But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".

Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls , Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.

China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power , drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.

national.title: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
national.summary: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez wants to defy the polls, and his main rivals accuse him of not telling the truth and of "betrayal".
national.body:
Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.

"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right.

Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".

He accused Sánchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.

The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.

Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.

"This time, yes, we're going to do it," Feijóo told PP supporters, in a nod to his failure to form a government three years ago despite winning most seats.

If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in front of thousands of people in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.

national.title: Mexico's government is slamming a DEA crime tip line as foreign interference. Others are thrilled.
national.summary: The announcement opened the latest chapter in an ongoing struggle between the U.S. and Mexican governments over who has the right to take action against cartels in Mexico.
national.body:
Fabiola Sanchez, Associated Press Fabiola Sanchez, Associated Press

MEXICO CITY (AP) — The government in Mexico is railing against the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency's anonymous tip line for reports against criminals and corrupt officials in the Latin American nation, slamming it as foreign interference.

In the state of Sinaloa, journalist Juan Manuel Partida Valdez was among the first to write to the WhatsApp line on Thursday, just a day after DEA chief Terry Cole called for anonymous reports on his X account.

The announcement opened the latest chapter in an ongoing struggle between the U.S. and Mexican governments over who has the right to take action against cartels in Mexico.

Partida Valdez, president of the Sinaloa Journalists Association, said he sent information about alleged ties between Sinaloa politicians and criminal groups because authorities have failed to put an end to violence and corruption that has bled his northern Mexican region dry in recent years.

"I talk to so many people — in the streets, on social media, on WhatsApp and in chats — and you realize what people think: We're all fed up," the 67-year-old told The Associated Press on Friday. "We're fed up with narco-governments."

On Friday, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said she escalated her fight with Washington over the tip line, filing a formal complaint with the U.S. Embassy for interfering in Mexico's internal affairs.

"We have made it very clear in our relationship with the United States that the relationship is one of coordination, not subordination," Sheinbaum said in her morning press briefing.

national.title: 25-year sentence sought for former chef who aided 14 suicides
national.summary: Kenneth Law pleaded guilty earlier this year to aiding 14 suicides in Canada, but he has admitted to selling his so-called suicide kits globally.
national.body: Canadian prosecutors on Friday requested a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold poison to help people die by suicide, stressing his victims were largely young and experiencing mental distress. Former chef Kenneth Law pleaded guilty earlier this year to aiding 14 suicides in Canada, but he has admitted to selling his so-called suicide kits globally through a series of online forums. Prosecutors had also charged him with murder but, citing a lack of evidence, agreed to withdraw the more serious accusations in exchange for Law pleading guilty to lesser offenses. That decision drew widespread condemnation, notably from friends and family of victims who believed Law was directly responsible for killing their loved ones, but prosecutors maintained they would still seek a stiff penalty. "An appropriate global sentence to impose in this matter is 25 years less (time already served)," Crown prosecutor Katie Doherty told the court. Courts often use comparable cases in determining sentencing, but Doherty noted there is "no case even remotely similar to Mr Law's conduct." The Canadian public was shocked when the breadth of Law's operation was revealed following his arrest. He sold poison to people in at least 41 countries, including China, France, and Brazil. He sold 330 packages to people in the United Kingdom, according to an agreed statement of facts signed by the defense and prosecution. national.title: Canada's Supreme Court largely upholds a Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
national.summary: The 2019 law, known as Bill 21, bans religious symbols — including Muslim headscarves, Sikh turbans, Jewish skullcaps and Christian crosses — for workers covered by it.
national.body:
TORONTO (AP) — Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld most of a Quebec law banning public schoolteachers, police officers and other public employees in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols at work. The ruling affirmed Quebec's power to override certain constitutional rights to keep the ban in place.

The 2019 law, known as Bill 21, bans religious symbols — including Muslim headscarves, Sikh turbans, Jewish skullcaps and Christian crosses — for workers covered by it.

Canada has long embraced multiculturalism, encouraging people to retain their cultural and religious identities. Supporters of Quebec's ban say public officials should avoid wearing religious symbols to demonstrate government neutrality.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon welcomed the ruling as "a victory for secularism" and for Quebec's ability to make different choices from the rest of Canada.

The court upheld Quebec's use of the "notwithstanding clause," which allows lawmakers to override certain rights, including religious freedom and equality. Those rights are protected by the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, Canada's equivalent of the U.S. Bill of Rights. Lawmakers must renew the override every five years to keep it in effect.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said he respected the ruling but pledged that his government would not use the constitutional override. He stressed that constitutional rights are particularly important for minorities and vulnerable people.

"Canada is a mosaic," Carney said, adding that it represents more than different backgrounds and identities. "It's a commitment, in my judgment, a commitment to how we treat each other."

Carney also welcomed the court's finding that judges can still declare that a law violates constitutional rights even when the override allows it to remain in force. He said that scrutiny helps inform Canadians and is useful in a democracy.

The detonation of the nation's aging stockpile of lead azide, which spurred widespread concerns about potential environmental contamination, has been deemed a success by the U.S. Army. But questions remain about how and when the federal government communicated its plans.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said about 300 people spent Thursday in the field sampling schools, playgrounds, churches and homes across the region. Results were expected in the coming days.

More than 1,500 samples were taken of air, water, soil and dust before the detonation. After, they took hundreds of samples including from homes, parks and drinking water, the EPA has said.

So far, the EPA said there has continued to be "zero" airborne lead detected in the region since Wednesday's controlled detonation.

While that's reassuring, residents and some elected officials have criticized the Army for not being more transparent and providing more notice when it first determined the stockpile was unstable.

A notice that plant managers planned to neutralize the stockpile was posted on a government website. Growing concern led to a plant closure in March that was publicized, and an October public meeting warned that the chemicals would soon need to be detonated.

national.title: Marching bands scramble to cover NYC costs after parade rearranged
national.summary: Stormy weather in New York City prompted organisers to push back the Macy's parade by two days - leaving some musicians stuck.
national.body:
Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.

"It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people.

Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (£267,000) in just a few hours.

Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.

On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.

The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.

The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.

Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. military has disabled a merchant ship in the Gulf of Oman that was trying to run its blockade of Iranian ports, U.S. Central Command said Friday.

A military aircraft fired "precision munitions" at the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer on Thursday, and the "ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed," it said in a statement.

According to U.S. Central Command, the Pacific Archer left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas before it attempted to run the blockade. Ship tracking websites list the vessel's destination as Singapore.

The commander of the Iranian navy, Shahram Irani, said Friday on state television that Iran will carry out operations "that will not only break the naval blockade but also drive the enemy out of the region's waters."

The strike comes as the Trump administration weighs its options in the long-simmering war with Iran, which began at the end of February and has settled into a quiet stalemate in the past several months.

Earlier in November, officials in the region told The Associated Press that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was pushing the U.S. to restart the war or allow Israel to launch airstrikes on Iran's nuclear facilities and missile capabilities.

national.title: Using a drone and a poop-sniffing dog, scientists perform health checks on endangered orcas
national.summary: In their search for their dwindling food source, the whales are spending less time in the Salish Sea, the maze of inland waters between Washington State and British Columbia.
national.body:
Manuel Valdes, Associated Press Manuel Valdes, Associated Press

KINGSTON, Wash. (AP) — Every fall for the last few years, Deborah Giles starts her work day with one question in mind: Where are the orcas?

Giles is tracking the Southern Resident killer whales, an endangered species whose population recovery is faltering despite years of protection. In their search for their dwindling food source, the whales are spending less time in the Salish Sea, the maze of inland waters between Washington State and British Columbia. But in the last half-decade, the orcas have been hunting coho and chum salmon just north of Seattle during the fall.

It's providing an opportunity for collaboration between The SeaDoc Society and the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. They're using drones mounted with petri dishes and microscope slides to collect droplets from whale spouts and employing a poop-sniffing dog to find stool samples, providing much-needed wellness checks for as many of the 76 remaining whales as they can find.

"They were here before us, long before us," said Giles. "They're a group of animals that are uniquely bonded to this place and to each other."

A research drone flown by Dr. James Sheppard of the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance hovers over K33 "Tika," a Southern Resident killer whale, while attempting to collect breath samples, on Puget Sound near Possession Point State Park, Washington, on Nov. 18, 2026. Photo by Lindsey Wasson/AP (NMFS/NOAA permit #26288-01)

Before colonization of the Pacific Northwest, the orca's main prey — Chinook salmon — could weigh more than 100 pounds (45.36 kilograms) and their numbers were abundant along the West Coast, Giles said.

But when American settlers came to the region, they built dams and overfished salmon. As cities and ports grew, boats created more noise, hindering the orca's hunting. Toxic chemicals flowed into sea water. And Chinook salmon now average about 12.5 pounds (5.66 kilograms), Giles said.

national.title: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter
national.summary: Ukraine settles in for another devastating winter as the questions persists: how will it all end?
national.body:
Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

national.title: A Ukraine loan is in limbo after EU budget talks stall. Leaders will try again
national.summary: The spending package is small compared to national budgets — around 1% to 1.2% of gross national income — but it encapsulates the ambitions of the world's biggest trading bloc and how it sees itself on the international stage.
national.body:
BRUSSELS (AP) — After struggling to chaperone Europe's leaders through more than 12 hours of high-stakes budget negotiations, European Council President António Costa faced reporters early Friday with a stark assessment. "We didn't reach an agreement," he said.

Government leaders from the 27-nation European Union failed to narrow down the size of the 2028-2034 budget — let alone how it might be used. An important loan for Ukraine was caught up in the wrangling.

The spending package is small compared to national budgets — around 1% to 1.2% of gross national income — but it encapsulates the ambitions of the world's biggest trading bloc and how it sees itself on the international stage.

Costa said "some member states asked for further reductions" in how much they would have to pay in, according to his latest proposals, while most were "opposed to further cuts, and some even proposed to reverse some cuts."

It was a day of brinksmanship that saw the leaders playing tough for national audiences.

In three weeks, they will try again. The stakes are high. Elections in some key countries are approaching, and new hardline governments or shaky coalitions could complicate matters further.

In coming days, Costa will draw his conclusions from the summit talks — held in two plenary sessions, several group meetings, and the corridor conversations that typify EU budget negotiations — and consult again with capitals.

Some leaders, notably from countries that pay more into the budget than they get back in allocations, skipped certain meetings. But Costa, a former Portuguese prime minister, was unruffled.

local.title: FOTI: Safer roads are a shared responsibility
local.summary: One of the most important responsibilities of county government is providing safe, reliable roads and bridges for the people who use them every day. As Chairman of the Niagara County Legislature’s Infrastructure Committee, I work with our Department of Public…
local.body:
One of the most important responsibilities of county government is providing safe, reliable roads and bridges for the people who use them every day. As Chairman of the Niagara County Legislature’s Infrastructure Committee, I work with our Department of Public Works to ensure that maintaining our transportation infrastructure and improving traffic safety are at the top of our priority list. We recognize that every intersection, every stretch of roadway and every traffic-control decision can have a real impact on the safety of our residents.

Just as importantly, we listen when residents raise concerns. People who travel our roads every day often recognize potential problems and hazards that deserve attention. We take those concerns seriously, work with our municipal partners and rely on professional engineering guidance to determine the appropriate solutions.

Shawn Foti is a Niagara County Legislator representing the 14th District which includes Newfane, Somerset and part of the Town of Lockport.

local.title: New bill aims to keep AI out of court opinions
local.summary: New legislation introduced in the state Senate aims to keep artificial intelligence from being used in court opinions in New York. Sen. Michelle Hinchey, D-Kingston, recently introduced legislation (S.10741) that would add a new section to the state Judiciary Law that would prohibit judges from usin
local.body:
New legislation introduced in the state Senate aims to keep artificial intelligence from being used in court opinions in New York.

Sen. Michelle Hinchey, D-Kingston, recently introduced legislation (S.10741) that would add a new section to the state Judiciary Law that would prohibit judges from using fabricated legal authority in adjudicative writings. Hinchey proposes making knowledgeable use or reckless use of AI by judges professional misconduct.

The state's Unified Court System recently released its Interim Policy on the Use of Artificial Intelligence. In October 2025, Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, spoke on the Senate floor to discuss his oversight of federal judges' AI use after finding two federal judges whose court staff used AI to draft inaccurate court orders that the judges approved. During his floor speech, Grassley called on every federal judge, the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts and the Judicial Conference to develop formal measures and meaningful guidance to prevent future AI misuse.

"New York should not wait for comparable judicial failures to cause harm in this state," Hinchey wrote in her legislative justification. "This bill will establish a clear rule of judicial accountability before such misconduct causes substantial harm in New York, while preserving lawful and responsible uses of AI."

Hinchey's bill would state that a judge who knowingly or recklessly includes, relies on or adopts fabricated legal authority as part of adjudicative writing is engaging in misconduct. The use of AI by a judge would not, by itself, constitute misconduct, however. A judge would not be found guilty of misconduct if the errors are based solely on good-faith interpretation, immaterial typographic or clerical errors, or other immaterial errors that can be corrected quickly without adverse consequences.

The state Commission on Judicial Conduct would be required to consider the number and materiality of fabricated authorities; whether errors affected the disposition of the case; applicable verification procedures or training received; and whether the error was repeated or promptly corrected when deciding whether a judge has committed judicial misconduct with the use of AI.

A Northwestern University study released earlier this year surveying federal judges across the U.S. on their use and outlook on artificial intelligence in and outside of the courtroom found that more than 60% of judges who responded reported using at least one AI tool in their judicial work. While judges reported broad adoption of AI tools, only 22.4% of judges reported using AI tools on a weekly or daily basis.

local.title: Sheriff details opposition to Local Cops, Local Crimes Act
local.summary: As Chautauqua County Sheriff, my responsibility is to protect everyone who lives here and to uphold the Constitution. Those duties are not in conflict. Public safety is strongest when law enforcement follows due process, treats people fairly and earns the community’s trust. I oppose the Local Cops,
local.body:
As Chautauqua County Sheriff, my responsibility is to protect everyone who lives here and to uphold the Constitution. Those duties are not in conflict. Public safety is strongest when law enforcement follows due process, treats people fairly and earns the community's trust.

I oppose the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act because I believe New York should not unnecessarily limit local agencies' ability to work with federal partners. But the distinction at the heart of this debate matters: we should not detain someone solely on a civil immigration warrant or detainer after the person is otherwise entitled to be released. A civil immigration document is not the same as a judicial warrant. We should continue to honor valid judicial warrants and court orders, and to work with federal authorities on criminal matters.

Our community includes immigrants who have lawfully entered the United States and people pursuing established immigration and asylum processes. They deserve due process and the same confidence that they can report crimes, serve as witnesses and seek help without being treated as suspects because of their background. Protecting that trust helps keep the whole community safe.

That principle does not require turning away from legitimate law-enforcement partnerships. The Sheriff's Office has a longstanding agreement with the U.S. Marshals Service to house federal prisoners charged with or convicted of federal crimes, as well as material witnesses. That is criminal detention – not confinement for a civil immigration violation. Our work with U.S. Border Patrol has also focused on border security and public safety. These partnerships should be judged by what they actually authorize and do, not blurred together with civil immigration enforcement.

The law itself recognizes some of these distinctions: it allows local agencies to contract to detain people facing federal criminal charges and to comply with judicial warrants and court orders, while requiring counties to end agreements covering civil immigration detention by November 2026. My concern is that a broad state mandate can restrict local decision-making and create uncertainty about partnerships that serve legitimate public-safety purposes.

There is also a question New Yorkers deserve a clear answer to: What has been the Department of Corrections and Community Supervision's policy for transferring incarcerated noncitizens to ICE, and how was that policy applied during the 2025 correction officers' strike? DOCCS describes a parole option for certain incarcerated people with a final deportation order who have waived or exhausted their appeals. A state appellate court has also said DOCCS may not hold someone beyond their release date solely to facilitate a transfer to immigration authorities. The public deserves a straightforward account of how those rules were applied during the strike, including whether any transfers occurred and under what authority.

local.title: Conservancy awarded $1.3M grant for protection of Cattaraugus County forest
local.summary: The Western New York Land Conservancy was recently awarded a major grant toward the permanent protection of roughly 400 acres in Randolph, Cattaraugus County. In 2027 the Land Conservancy will be fundraising to raise the final $450,000 in hopes of permanently protecting this beautiful property. This
local.body:
The Western New York Land Conservancy was recently awarded a major grant toward the permanent protection of roughly 400 acres in Randolph, Cattaraugus County. In 2027 the Land Conservancy will be fundraising to raise the final $450,000 in hopes of permanently protecting this beautiful property. This project is thanks in part to $1.3 million through the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation, Open Space Conservation Grant Program through appropriations from the New York State Environmental Protection Fund (EPF) and Clean Water, Clean Air, and Green Jobs Environmental Bond Act.

The parcel is largely forested, featuring rich hemlock-hardwood forests along steep slopes and ravines. Many headwater tributaries flow down the steep grade of the property and feed into Little Conewango Creek and the Allegheny River. Protecting these forests and waterways will help safeguard water quality, groundwater resources, and aquatic habitat throughout the region.

The property is part of the 853-acre Camp Timbercrest, owned by Girl Scouts of Western New York. As they prepare to celebrate 60 years of outdoor programs at Timbercrest in August 2027, the Land Conservancy is working with Girl Scouts to acquire and permanently protect the wildland portion of the property that does not contain camp buildings and infrastructure.

"Protecting Timbercrest is an investment in the long-term health of our region's forests, waterways, wildlife, and communities," said Marisa Riggi, Executive Director of the Western New York Land Conservancy. "This grant will help us permanently conserve an important piece of Western New York's natural landscape while creating new opportunities for people to experience and enjoy nature."

This partnership represents a win-win for conservation and Girl Scouts, deepening the commitment of Girl Scouts of Western New York to be good stewards of their resources and provide generations of Western New Yorkers with access to protected lands. The sale of this large, undeveloped section of the camp will ensure that the land itself remains protected forever while Girl Scouts of Western New York continues to provide high quality youth outdoor programs. Through this partnership, Girl Scouts of Western New York will grow the impact of their mission while preserving the forests, streams, and wildlife habitat that make Timbercrest such a special place.

For the Land Conservancy, Timbercrest's location makes it especially valuable for conservation. The property borders the 1,142-acre Pine Hill State Forest, which connects to the 4,246-acre South Valley State Forest, Allegany State Park, and the Allegheny National Forest. It is also near the 377-acre Janet Gallogly Allegany Wildlands, which they've already purchased and permanently protected.

local.title: Some deer are immortal: Big game hunting in WNY
local.summary: In Western New York, the regular deer season is more than a date range on the calendar. It’s a family reunion with blaze orange, a little fresh air, and occasionally a thermos of coffee that tastes suspiciously like last year’s. For archery hunters, the Southern Zone season begins early on October 1
local.body:
In Western New York, the regular deer season is more than a date range on the calendar. It's a family reunion with blaze orange, a little fresh air, and occasionally a thermos of coffee that tastes suspiciously like last year's.

For archery hunters, the Southern Zone season begins early on October 1. Firearms hunters had to wait until Nov. 21, this year, when the regular season opened. It will close Dec. 13. That's a long wait, but the anticipation is half the fun. New York's busiest deer-hunting week arrives each year with the opening of firearms season, when hundreds of thousands of hunters head for the woods.

What a gathering it is! Generations of hunters, old friends, young apprentices, and the occasional relative who claims he saw a twelve-point buck but somehow forgot his camera. Every hunting clan has one.

The best part of the start of firearm reason is that the rut is underway. Bucks are searching for does, and modern deer calls and scents can sometimes convince a curious buck that romance is just around the next tree. He approaches, stops, approaches again. Then he catches a scent that you may have planted and trots closer.

The experienced hunter knows the difference between an exciting opportunity and a safe, ethical shot. A running deer is neither a sure thing nor a good reason to pull the trigger. Sometimes a quiet whistle or grunt brings him to a stop. Sometimes he bolts and disappears into the timber, leaving only a memory and a story that begins, "You should have seen him!"

That's the beauty of it. The greatest deer stories aren't always about the biggest antlers. They're about the cold morning, the first deer a youngster saw, the friend who shared his lunch, or the buck that finally stepped into view after hours of patience. Details matter.

When a deer is harvested, the story takes on another responsibility. A legal harvest deserves respect. Make a careful recovery, use the animal as fully as possible, follow New York's tagging and reporting requirements, and never let the excitement overshadow the life taken. Venison shared around the table is a meaningful way to honor the animal and the effort behind your hunt. No waste.

New York's regular-season bag limit is one antlered deer on the regular-season tag. Additional deer may be taken with valid tags, such as Deer Management Permits, subject to specific rules for a multiple number of Wildlife Management Units. Always check the regulations for your Wildlife Management Unit and license.

SILVER CREEK -- At its most recent meeting, the Silver Creek Village Board commended the Silver Creek VFW and the Town of Hanover for their events held on Veterans Day. Mayor Kathy Tampio called the Town's Veterans Memorial "a great way to remember and appreciate our veterans."

While singling out the efforts of Town Clerk Elizabeth VanCheri, Supervisor Lou Pelletter, and Town Board member Aimee Rogers, Tampio said, "The Town of Hanover did a wonderful job."

Later in the meeting, recently re-elected Village Trustees Dwayne Haskins and Mary Poissant thanked voters for their support in the November election. Haskins and Poissant were each re-elected in some of the only truly competitive races throughout the county. Their fellow Board members offered congratulations at the latest meeting.

Poissant is involved with the newly formed Place Making Committee for community activism. At its latest meeting, County officials stated that a mural is set to move forward in Silver Creek. More information will be made available in the coming months.

Several local residents have also formed a historic preservation group whose focus is on protecting the unique buildings and monuments in the community. The group is looking to establish an official name and mission statement in the coming weeks.

Also of note, the Village recently met with the engineers handling the Buffalo Street improvement project. The Village will provide updates at a later date.

The Silver Creek Emergency Squad responded to 51 incidents in the month of October.

The next meeting of the Silver Creek Village Board will be held on Monday, Dec. 7 at 7 p.m. in the Village Boardroom.

local.title: Stepping up
local.summary: ORCHARD PARK — Choppy as the game was played and sloppy as the conditions were, the Buffalo Bills showed they can win on one of Josh Allen’s worst days. Though the Bills need their star to regain his groove, Buffalo’s 13-10 win over the Kansas City Chiefs on a cold, wet and windy Thursday night […]
local.body:
AP Photo Buffalo Bills place kicker Tyler Bass walks off the field after defeating the Kansas City Chiefs 13-10 in Orchard Park on Thursday night.

AP Photo Kansas City Chiefs wide receiver Rashee Rice (4) has a ball knocked from him by Buffalo Bills safety Amani Hooker (22) during the second half of Thursday's game in Orchard Park.

ORCHARD PARK -- Choppy as the game was played and sloppy as the conditions were, the Buffalo Bills showed they can win on one of Josh Allen’s worst days.

Though the Bills need their star to regain his groove, Buffalo’s 13-10 win over the Kansas City Chiefs on a cold, wet and windy Thursday night shined light on why this year’s team might be better equipped to fulfill its long-elusive Super Bowl aspirations.

The defense -- questioned over the past month for beating up on backups and third-stringers -- just may be for real. Buffalo limited Patrick Mahomes and the NFL’s top offense to 10 points and 241 yards, forced five three-and-outs and a season-best seven punts.

And Buffalo’s special teams finally gained the recognition they deserve for being a difference-maker in securing the victory, and after spending much of the season hovering under the radar.

With Allen flailing and looking indecisive, Buffalo’s other two units bailed him out, capped by a key sequence of plays over the final 38 seconds.

It began with punter Tommy Doman pinning the Chiefs at their 11 -- the rookie landed three of his five kicks inside Kansas City’s 20. The defense then did its part by forcing a three-and-out. With Buffalo’s Joe Andreessen appearing to tip Matt Araiza’s punt, Greg Dortch fielded the line-drive kick and returned it 17 yards to set up Tyler Bass hitting the decisive 57-yard field goal as time expired.

Audrey A. (Wilemski) McGill, 79, of Dunkirk, is at rest after a valiant fight with cancer on November 22, 2026. She was born in Dunkirk on December 29, 1946, she was the loving and caring wife of Danny McGill for 55 years.

Audrey graduated from Dunkirk High School, Class of 1964. She was employed by M. Wile for many years until its closing and later worked as a cleaner for the Dunkirk City School District.

Audrey faced her battle with cancer with courage, strength, and faith. An avid animal lover, she opened her heart and home to numerous stray cats over the years, giving them the love and care they deserved. She found enjoyment in watching beautiful sunsets and tending to her vegetable garden. Audrey was a member of the Dunkirk Senior Center and a parishioner of Blessed Mary Angela Church of St. Hyacinth.

Her family would like to extend a special thank you to her niece, Theresa Schrantz, Chautauqua Hospice & Palliative Care, and the staff at Chautauqua Nursing & Rehabilitation Center for the exceptional care, compassion, and kindness shown to Audrey.Audrey is survived by her loving husband of 55 years, Danny McGill, her best friend and twin sister, Ardene Lesch, her sister-in-law Patricia A. Kaus. She is also survived by many nieces and nephews.

She is predeceased by her parents Frank and Rose (Kaus) Wilemski, her sister Bernadette Pasiecznik and her brother Ronald R. Kaus.

Funeral services will be held privately at the convenience of the family. Interment will be held privately in St. Hedwig's Cemetery Columbarium. Arrangements are by R. Michael Mackowiak III; R. Mackowiak Funeral Home, Inc., 56 East Doughty Street, Dunkirk, NY. Share condolences at, www.Rmackowiak.com

Memorial contributions in Audrey's memory may be made to St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, Shriners Hospitals for Children, or the Chautauqua Humane Society.

local.title: 3 men spend week living on streets of Buffalo to raise awareness about homelessness
local.summary: Three young men are spending the week living on the streets of Buffalo and are hoping to raise awareness about the struggles of homelessness and encourage others to help people in need.
local.body: Three young men are spending the week living on the streets of Buffalo and are hoping to raise awareness about the struggles of homelessness and encourage others to help people in need.Alex Johns, Nate Johns and their cousin, Tommy Rutherford, all involved with the Buffalo Dream Center, are spending seven days living outdoors alongside Buffalo's homeless community.For Alex Johns, one of the biggest challenges has been finding a safe and warm place to rest."One of the most challenging things is just finding that warm place to stay, trying to stay dry and getting a good night's sleep. It's actually pretty more challenging than people think," Alex said.Tommy Rutherford said a difficult night outdoors helped put the purpose of the experience into perspective."Got wet last night and we were sleeping outside, and it was kind of, it was rough," Rutherford said. "You know, we're out here, we're in the shoes of the people that are in need, that are on the streets. I feel like this really shows the significance of this week and the need in our city."Nate Johns has been involved in street ministry with his father, Rev. Eric Johns, pastor of the Buffalo Dream Center, for years. He said spending time outdoors has given him a different perspective on the conversations he has with people experiencing homelessness."Yeah, there's something about walking in another man's shoes and actually being in the environment. I actually was able to talk to a few men today. And they made a point of saying, 'Man, you guys really come out here, and you're in the elements with everybody else. And now you know what it's like,'" Nate said.WATCH: 3 men spend week living on streets of Buffalo to raise awareness about homelessnessThe effort comes as homelessness remains a concern across Western New York. local.title: Severe ice and wind leaves more than 3,000 Cattaraugus Co. residents without power
local.summary: Powerful winds and extensive ice have downed multiple power lines, leaving over 3,000 customers in Cattaraugus County without power.
local.body: Powerful winds and extensive ice have downed multiple power lines, leaving over 3,000 customers in Cattaraugus County without power.As of 3 p.m. on Friday, National Grid crews are continuing to clear downed lines, and 100 active outages are still being reported.According to the Cattaraugus County Office of Emergency Services, National Grid expects the majority of those customers will likely be without power until late this evening, although there are no official "ERTs" (estimated restoration times)."A lot of it was just being overwhelmed all at once," Farmersville EMS Captain Elizabeth Mann told WKBW. "We just kind of had to catch up and go from there." The Farmersville Fire Department has received 32 calls since 4:45 p.m. on Thursday."It just got cold, started raining, everything iced over, and all the trees started tipping over," Farmersville resident Daniel Koch Jr. recounted to WKBW. Koch's power remains out as well. "The refrigerator is getting warm. With the generator running, so that's where we're at.""Might take a trip to Olean," Koch said. "They got power over there," Koch said.While sympathetic to residents remaining in the dark, Mann encourages anyone in the affected areas to travel only if necessary."Trees are still coming down, and power lines are still coming down around us, so the more that you can stay indoors helps us be able to do our jobs better."The EMS captain added, "Definitely check on your elderly residents or elderly neighbors, family members, do the best you can to kind of check in on them, make sure that they have what they need, and stay indoors for the most part."Additionally, National Grid encourages everyone experiencing a power outage to contact their power company to report the outage. Even if your neighbor reported it or you see crews working in your area, still call to report and ensure your address is logged in their system. local.title: State Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins has died
local.summary: She was the first woman and first African-American woman to serve as Senate Majority Leader, one of the most powerful positions in state government.
local.body:
State Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins, a Yonkers Democrat who made history as the first Black woman to lead a legislative conference in Albany, died unexpectedly on Friday. She was 76.

Stewart-Cousins’ longtime spokesperson, Mike Murphy, confirmed her death. The cause was not immediately clear.

Her passing comes less than two weeks after Senate Democrats voted to give her another two-year term as majority leader, one of the three most powerful positions in New York state government.

It sent shockwaves through the state Capitol, where Stewart-Cousins was a towering figure who played an outsize role in all substantial legislation that has passed since Democrats took control of the Senate in 2018.

“Andrea was more than just a remarkable public servant,” said Westchester County Executive Ken Jenkins, a longtime Stewart-Cousins ally. “She was a trailblazer, a dedicated advocate for the people of our county, and a leader whose impact will continue to be felt for generations.”

First elected to the Senate in 2006, Stewart-Cousins steadily rose through the ranks before her Democratic colleagues elected her minority leader in 2012.

Over time, she steadied what had been a tumultuous conference rocked by infighting and scandal. Under her watch, Democrats won enough seats over several election cycles to retake the Senate majority in 2018, knocking Republicans from the majority perch they had held for the better part of a century and making Stewart-Cousins the first woman to lead the Senate.

Since then, Stewart-Cousins was one of three people — along with the governor and Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie — to negotiate state budgets and major pieces of legislation. As leader, she helped pass bills to strengthen state abortion protections and reform the criminal-justice system, including a dramatic reduction in the number of crimes subject to cash bail.

entertainment.summary: Cam Gigandet is back on the hunt. Eighteen years after Gigandet famously uttered, "you brought a snack" at the Cullens' baseball game in Twilight, he transformed into a biker bad boy named Gentle...
entertainment.body:
Eighteen years after Gigandet famously uttered, "you brought a snack" at the Cullens' baseball game in Twilight , he transformed into a biker bad boy named Gentle John Moffitt for season two of Hunting Wives .

Instead of luring Kristen Stewart 's Bella into an empty ballet studio to suck her blood as villainous vampire James, Gigandet now plays the nephew of a gang leader named Zelda, portrayed by Widow's Bay star Dale Dickey . As Zelda seeks justice for the murder of her granddaughter, Gentle John works as her enforcer, seeking answers from Malin Akerman 's Margo Banks about her role in the disappearance.

And to become the duplicitous criminal onscreen, Gigandet ditched his signature dirty blonde tresses for a dark brown buzzcut and a disheveled beard. While taking on the gruff disposition of a small-town Southerner was a change of pace for the 44-year-old, it continued his streak of physical roles, like in 2008's Never Back Down and seasons three and four of The O.C .

In fact, the Easy A actor flexed his muscles in many action movies in more recent years. Gigandet starred in Love Hurts with Ke Huy Quan , Violent Night with David Harbour and Mafia Wars with Tom Welling .

Outside of life behind the camera, Gigandet was married to Dominique Gigandet from 2008 to 2022, and the pair share kids Everleigh , Rekker and Armie . Since his divorce from the spray tan artist , Gigandet began dating actress Hannah James in 2023, with whom he costarred in Two Sinners and a Mule the same year. entertainment.summary: "I don't have $6 million," the comedian later admitted. "And my wife wouldn't lend me any of her money."
entertainment.body:
Bob Newhart could make millions laugh, but a $6 million lawsuit was no laughing matter.

The comedy legend once tried to quit his hit CBS sitcom, “The Bob Newhart Show,” only to discover the network wasn’t ready to let its ratings star walk away.

The contract dispute is detailed in Michael Seth Starr’s biography, “Bob Newhart: The Life and Laughter of an American Treasure,” which chronicles the comedian’s nearly 65-year career.

Newhart wasn’t exactly in a position to face a multimillion-dollar lawsuit.

“I don’t have $6 million,” the comedian later admitted. “And my wife wouldn’t lend me any of her money.”

Although he publicly credited fan support for his decision, Newhart later acknowledged that financial pressure played a major role in his return.

“When I said I wanted to quit, the people in the cast and the production crew were all affected, of course and they helped influence me to change my mind. Then there were letters from fans and people I met on the street. But I guess the main reason I decided to come back was that CBS threatened to sue me for $6 million because there was a year left on my contract.”

According to Starr’s biography, Newhart approached CBS executives Bob Daly and Robert Wussler about leaving “The Bob Newhart Show” before its sixth season.

entertainment.title: Child actor Reggie Absolom takes swipe at JK Rowling after losing ‘Harry Potter’ role
entertainment.summary: “'Harry Potter' is out the window ... I think we don’t worry about it anymore,” Absolom said.
entertainment.body:
Child actor Reggie Absolom has come out swinging against author JK Rowling after missing out on a role in HBO’s upcoming television reboot of the “Harry Potter” franchise .

Absolom, 14, was reportedly in contention for a key role in the series and made it to the last round of auditions before ultimately losing out.

While Absolom didn’t make the cut, a casting director did pass the actor’s name around town, resulting in him landing a separate role in the upcoming drama film “Club Kid,” directed by Jordan Firstman.

When asked about losing the role in an interview with Variety , Absolom said he much preferred his time on “Club Kid” while taking a swipe at Rowling, the author of the “Harry Potter” books.

“’Harry Potter’ is out the window. ‘Harry Potter’ got me here, and I thank it for that. But I think we don’t worry about it anymore,” Absolom told Variety.

“I’d rather do [‘Club Kid’]. I loved everyone on this set. I had such a good time filming it, and I think JK Rowling is a no anyway, but Jordan Firstman is a big yes,” he added.

While Absolom didn’t get into specifics of why Rowling “is a no,”, the author’s controversial stance on transgender people has in recent years been criticized by multiple Hollywood names, including original “Harry Potter” castmates Daniel Radcliffe and Emma Watson .

Backlash over Rowling’s views resurfaced when HBO first announced its TV reboot series back in 2023, with multiple stars from the show, including John Lithgow, issuing responses after their casting .
